title: Their opinion, strangely
hookLine: we love ourselves most but trust others' opinion of us more than our own (Meditations 12.4)

cards: You've decided the outfit looks good. Then someone glances at it a certain way, and suddenly it doesn't. You were sure the idea was solid, until a coworker raised one eyebrow.

We spend every waking minute with ourselves, know our own reasons better than anyone, and still hand the verdict to whoever happens to be looking. Marcus noticed the same oddness, and wrote it down as a puzzle.

teach.b: I've often wondered, Marcus writes, how it is that every person loves himself more than anyone else, and yet sets less value on his own opinion of himself than on other people's opinion of him. Second, the test.
He proposes a thought experiment. Suppose a god, or a wise teacher, stood beside you and told you never to think anything you wouldn't say out loud the moment you thought it.
Nobody could bear it, he says, not even for a single day. Third, what that shows. We're more concerned with what our neighbors will think of us than with what we think of ourselves.
We guard the outside carefully and leave the inside to anyone.
We'll rewrite an email five times for how it sounds, and let a mean thought run all morning unchecked. Fourth, turning it around.
Marcus isn't saying other people's views never matter; a friend's honest criticism can be a gift. He's pointing at a strange imbalance.
The one person who's with you every minute, who knows your reasons and your efforts, gets the smallest vote.

how: People who draw on this passage sometimes pause before seeking reassurance and first ask what they themselves honestly think, then act on it when it's reasonable and kind.

o: the advice of experts, which Marcus said to always follow
gossip about us, which Marcus said to answer at once
what others think of us, which we oddly value above our own view

games.q: their opinion, strangely — tap the pairs.
p: love self most, trust others' view more
how long nobody could bear it

s: Marcus says other people's opinions never matter
he points at the imbalance, not at a friend's honest criticism.
he says no one could bear saying every thought aloud even for a day
that's his test of how much we care about appearances.

games.q: a god stands beside you and says: from now on, say every thought aloud as soon as you think it. what does Marcus think you'd do?
games.why: nobody could bear it even for a day, he writes, which shows we care more about what neighbors think of us than what we think of ourselves.

practice: Think of a choice you've been second-guessing because of what someone might think, a plan, a purchase, a thing you want to say, and set their imagined opinion aside.
Ask yourself honestly what you think, and whether it's reasonable and kind. If it is, let your own judgment stand, without asking anyone to approve it first.

wordCard.voice: Their opinion. Marcus's puzzle: we love ourselves most, yet value other people's opinion of us more than our own. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: my own opinion. Your honest look counts as much as the room's. Until tomorrow.
